answers.answer: A bucket is a container of objects. An object contains bytes and metadata; a key identifies it within its bucket. Object metadata describes the object, for example its content type, rather than application fields, relationships or ownership. In a flat namespace slashes are characters in one key; console folders group keys sharing a prefix. Changing a prefix changes affected names, commonly by copies and deletes, and is not an atomic directory rename. The API uploads report bytes to a bucket/key; the store holds bytes and object metadata, while the database holds application fields and the object reference. Retrieval reads that reference and requests the key. Upload and database commit are separate operations, not one transaction. Publish a ready reference only after confirming the intended object; an earlier pending record must not appear complete. An uncertain upload stays unresolved until verified. Upload success followed by database failure can leave an unreferenced object; premature publication can point to missing bytes. The application must recover by retrying reference publication or cleaning up an object established as no longer needed. Listing does not make the writes atomic.

evidence.quote: A container for objects. Each object contains bytes and metadata; its key identifies it within that bucket.
Console folders group keys by a shared beginning, called a prefix; they are not filesystem directories.
It is not one atomic directory rename.
The object upload and database commit are separate operations. The object store does not commit them together.
Confirm the intended object before making a reference available as ready to readers.
The application needs recovery, such as retrying reference publication or cleaning up an object it has established is no longer needed.

answers.answer: Supply a complete replacement at the same key even for a few changed bytes. S3 reads see a complete old or new object, never mixed bytes; GCS serves the old object until replacement completes and then the new one. The completed replacement is current, though an overlapping read may have seen the previous object. Atomic replacement does not stop another writer. With versioning and other retention disabled, do not expect the previous bytes to remain recoverable. These are product-specific guarantees; verify the chosen service and its operations.

evidence.quote: In the standard whole-object upload model, changing a few bytes means supplying a complete replacement at the same key.
S3 documents atomic updates to one key: a concurrent read sees the complete old or new object, never a mixture.
GCS likewise serves the old object until replacement completes, then the new one.
With versioning and other retention protections disabled, do not expect to retrieve the old object after replacement.
These are product-specific guarantees, not promises made by the object-storage label alone.

answers.answer: An exact-key read retrieves one known object; a prefix listing enumerates names sharing a beginning. Neither queries arbitrary application fields. Use application records or a suitable index to find all records owned by a customer with approved status. Listing and inspecting objects adds requests, transferred data and latency as the collection grows. Current S3/GCS promise strong read-after-write and listing consistency: with no intervening change, subsequent reads/listings reflect a successful upload. This is not universal and an HTTP cache can serve an older copy. Consistency concerns observed state, so a consistent request may still fail. Multiple listing pages are not promised to be a frozen snapshot during changes; neither listing nor a one-key update is a transaction across keys or the database. Overlapping writes cannot be ordered into a final value by response arrival alone; observe stored state under provider rules.

evidence.quote: An exact-key request retrieves one object. A prefix listing enumerates names with a shared beginning.
Use application records or a suitable index for that query; listing and inspecting many objects adds requests, transferred data and latency as the collection grows.
With no intervening change, a successful upload is reflected in subsequent reads and listings.
Consistency describes which state an operation observes; the request can still fail.
Separate pages are not promised to form one frozen snapshot while objects change.
When writes to one key overlap, response arrival order alone does not identify the final object.

answers.answer: Yes, the upload may finish even if its response is lost. An unconditional retry can overwrite a newer object placed at the same key by another writer. Before publishing a ready reference, establish that the expected object is stored through acknowledgment or verification of expected identity and content under documented semantics. Existence proves only some object is there. A later read describes the state observed, not necessarily the outcome of the original request, because another write may intervene. A conditional write checks its condition as part of the operation: supported create-if-absent protects an existing live object, and an expected-version condition permits replacement only of the intended version. Rejection does not prove your bytes are stored, and a lost conditional response remains uncertain. S3/GCS APIs and details differ; follow documented protection and recovery, not a universal retry recipe.

evidence.quote: An upload can finish even when its response never reaches the caller.
An unconditional retry can replace a newer object written by someone else at the same key.
Use an acknowledged result or verify the expected identity and content under the store's documented semantics.
Finding the key proves only that some object exists.
A later read describes the state it observes, not necessarily which earlier request produced it; another write can intervene.
Where supported, create-if-absent protects an existing live object from replacement. An expected-version condition allows replacement only of the version the caller intended.
A rejected condition does not prove your bytes are stored. A lost response to a conditional upload is still uncertain.

answers.answer: Durability concerns preserving stored data intact over time; availability concerns accessing it when requested. Durable bytes can be temporarily unreachable, and neither target proves acknowledgment reached the caller. Redundant storage protects against hardware failures. S3/GCS document redundant storage before confirming successful writes, but a completed server write and delivery of its response are separate events. Multiple devices in one zone do not necessarily protect against loss of that zone; check class and placement. Redundancy does not undo intentional overwrite/delete. Configured versioning can preserve older versions; retention/recovery features may preserve removed bytes. Check enabled protections, whether configuration changes took effect, and whether the needed bytes remain retained. Recovery is neither automatic nor permanent merely because durability is high.

evidence.quote: Concerns keeping stored data intact over time. Redundant storage protects against hardware failures.
S3 and GCS document storing data redundantly before confirming successful writes, but that completed server-side write does not ensure its response reaches the caller.
Neither a durability target nor an availability target proves that one particular upload response arrived.
Multiple devices in one zone do not necessarily protect against losing that whole zone.
Redundancy also does not undo an intentional overwrite or delete.
Check which protections are enabled, whether configuration changes have taken effect, and whether the needed data is still retained.

answers.answer: The store authorizes presented credentials against storage policies, without automatically reading application ownership records. The application must check that this user may access this resource before fetching bytes or granting download access. A broad API credential can retrieve someone else's object from a private bucket when that check is skipped. A hard-to-guess key is an identifier, not permission. Limit operations and resource scope to what is needed; broad credentials in untrusted clients let them directly bypass application restrictions within that scope. Do not assume immediate policy revocation: GCS documents propagation delay, and a changed display proves little about all requests. For media/exports fetched by key, use object storage. For frequently updated records queried by fields, use a database for fields, relationships and transactions. For a database engine doing small-range writes on an attached disk-like volume, use block storage. For shared directories and file operations across machines, use shared file storage. For popular static assets close to users, use a CDN to cache/deliver copies, reducing origin traffic and delivery latency. Object storage suits complete-object creation/replacement and key retrieval; whole-object replacement and request overhead make frequent small in-place edits a poor default. A bucket does not supply application record queries/transactions or user permission checks. Object storage can retain the authoritative durable origin behind a CDN; the CDN does not replace it or the database. Small objects are allowed; there is no strict minimum size. No gaps in the supplied lesson for these questions.

evidence.quote: The object store authorizes the credentials presented on a request against its policies. It does not automatically read your application's ownership records.
A private bucket can still return another user's object when the API uses a broad credential and skips the application's permission check.
A hard-to-guess key is still an identifier, not a permission check.
Keep broad storage credentials out of untrusted clients: those clients could otherwise use the credential directly and bypass application restrictions within its allowed scope.
GCS documents that granting and revoking access can take time to propagate.
Whole-object replacement and request overhead make it a poor default for frequent small in-place edits.
Fits application records, field queries, relationships and transactions.
Provides disk-like blocks on an attached volume.
Provides a filesystem interface with directories and file operations for multiple machines.
Object storage can hold the origin object. The CDN does not replace the authoritative durable copy or the application database.
Small objects are allowed too; there is no strict minimum size implied by this model.
